theory.overview: Parsing transforms a flat stream of tokens into a hierarchical tree structure—the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). While lexing answers 'what are the words?', parsing answers 'what is the grammatical structure?'. The AST captures the semantic relationships between tokens, representing operations, precedence, and nesting. Every compiler, interpreter, and static analyzer relies on parsing to understand code structure before execution or transformation.

sections.title: From Tokens to Trees
sections.content: Consider the expression `3 + 4 * 5`. As tokens: [3, +, 4, *, 5]. But this misses crucial information: multiplication has higher precedence than addition. The AST makes this explicit: a root `+` node with children `3` and a `*` subtree. The `*` node has children `4` and `5`. This tree structure ensures correct evaluation order and provides a clean representation for code transformation, optimization, and code generation.

sections.title: Grammar and Production Rules
sections.content: Programming languages are defined by formal grammars, typically in Backus-Naur Form (BNF) or Extended BNF (EBNF). A grammar consists of terminals (tokens from the lexer) and non-terminals (syntactic categories like Expression, Statement, Function). Production rules define how non-terminals expand: Expression → Term { (+|-) Term }. This recursive definition captures arithmetic with proper precedence—Term handles higher-precedence * and /, while Expression handles lower-precedence + and -.

sections.title: Recursive Descent Parsing
sections.content: Recursive descent is the most intuitive parsing technique—each non-terminal becomes a function. The parser class maintains a current token pointer and provides methods to consume expected tokens. For Expression, we first parse a Term, then while the next token is + or -, we consume it and parse another Term. This naturally handles left-associativity and produces correct precedence. Each parse method returns an AST node, building the tree bottom-up.
keyPoints: Lookahead token determines which rule to apply
Mutual recursion between rules (Expr calls Term, Term calls Factor, Factor may call Expr)
Predictive parsing with fixed lookahead (typically 1 token)

sections.title: AST Node Types
sections.content: A well-designed AST uses distinct node types for different language constructs. BinaryOp nodes have left/right children and an operator. Literal nodes store values. Identifier nodes store names. Block nodes contain statement lists. IfStmt nodes have condition, then-block, and optional else-block. FunctionDecl nodes have name, parameters, and body. This type hierarchy enables the compiler to handle each construct appropriately during analysis and code generation.

sections.title: Error Handling and Recovery
sections.content: Production parsers must handle syntax errors gracefully. Synchronization points (like semicolons or closing braces) help the parser recover and continue finding more errors. Error messages should be specific: 'Expected ; after expression' is better than 'Syntax error'. Panic mode recovery skips tokens until a synchronizing token is found, allowing the parser to report multiple errors in one pass.

examples.recovery: Insert implicit parens or skip to '{'

keyConcepts.name: Left Recursion
keyConcepts.description: Rules like Expr → Expr + Term cause infinite recursion in naive recursive descent. Transform to Expr → Term { + Term } or use a loop.

keyConcepts.name: Operator Precedence
keyConcepts.description: Grammar structure encodes precedence: deeper rules (Term inside Expr) have higher precedence than outer rules.
keyConcepts.example: * binds tighter than + because Factor is inside Term which is inside Expr

keyConcepts.name: Associativity
keyConcepts.description: Left-associative: a - b - c = (a - b) - c. Right-associative: a = b = c = a = (b = c). Loop gives left, recursion gives right.
keyConcepts.example: Left recursion via loop; right recursion via recursive call

keyConcepts.name: LL(1) Grammars
keyConcepts.description: Grammars parseable with 1-token lookahead. First and Follow sets determine predictability. Most programming languages are designed to be LL(1) or close to it.
keyConcepts.check: No FIRST/FIRST conflicts, no FIRST/FOLLOW conflicts

complexity.timeComplexity: $O(n)$ for LL(1) recursive descent where $n$ = token count

steps.title: Initialize Parser
steps.description: Load tokens from lexer, set current position to first token, prepare error list.

steps.title: Parse Expression
steps.description: Entry point for parsing. Calls parseTerm for higher precedence, then handles + and -.

steps.title: Parse Term (Higher Precedence)
steps.description: Parse factors first, then handle * and /. This ensures * happens before +.

steps.title: Parse Factor (Base Case)
steps.description: Handle literals, identifiers, and parenthesized expressions. Returns leaf nodes.

steps.title: Build BinaryOp Node
steps.description: After parsing left and right operands, create BinaryOp AST node with operator.

steps.title: Return Completed AST
steps.description: Root node contains entire program structure. Ready for semantic analysis or code generation.

practiceProblems.title: Simple Expression AST
practiceProblems.explanation: Multiplication has higher precedence, so 3*2 forms a subtree. The + node has 5 and the * subtree as children.

practiceProblems.title: Parentheses Change Structure
practiceProblems.explanation: Parentheses force 5+3 to evaluate first. The * node now has the + subtree and 2 as children.
hints: + subtree is now left child of *

practiceProblems.title: AST Node Count
practiceProblems.description: How many AST nodes for: `a + b + c`?
practiceProblems.answer: 5 nodes: 2 BinaryOp nodes (+), 3 Identifier nodes (a, b, c)
practiceProblems.explanation: Left-associative: (a + b) + c. Two BinaryOp nodes (both +), three leaf Identifier nodes.

practiceProblems.title: Left vs Right Associativity
practiceProblems.description: How does AST differ for left-associative `a - b - c` vs right-associative `a = b = c`?
practiceProblems.answer: Left: ((- a b) c), Right: (a (= b c))
practiceProblems.explanation: Left-assoc builds left-deep tree. Right-assoc (assignment) builds right-deep tree. Evaluation order differs.

practiceProblems.title: Precedence Depth
practiceProblems.answer: Height 3 (root + or -, children include * and / subtrees at height 2, leaves at height 1)
practiceProblems.explanation: + and - are at same precedence level (left to right), * and / are deeper. Structure: (+ (- 1 (* 2 3)) (/ 4 5)) approx.
hints: Count edges from root to deepest leaf

practiceProblems.title: Grammar Production
practiceProblems.description: In grammar: Expr → Term { (+|-) Term }, what does { } mean?
practiceProblems.explanation: The braces indicate the (+|-) Term part can repeat zero or more times, enabling chains like a + b - c + d.

practiceProblems.title: First and Follow Sets
practiceProblems.description: Why do LL(1) parsers need FIRST and FOLLOW sets?
practiceProblems.answer: To determine which production to use with only 1-token lookahead
practiceProblems.explanation: FIRST tells what terminals a production can start with. FOLLOW tells what can follow a non-terminal. Together they resolve choice conflicts.
hints: FIRST: starting terminals of a rule

practiceProblems.title: Recursive Descent Advantage
practiceProblems.description: What makes recursive descent parsers easy to understand and implement?
practiceProblems.answer: Each grammar rule becomes a function—direct correspondence between grammar and code
practiceProblems.explanation: The structure mirrors the grammar exactly. Easy to debug, extend, and maintain. Hand-written parsers often use this approach.

practiceProblems.title: Parse Tree vs AST
practiceProblems.description: What's the difference between a parse tree and an AST?
practiceProblems.answer: Parse tree shows all grammar productions; AST is simplified, omits syntactic sugar
practiceProblems.explanation: Parse tree includes intermediate non-terminals. AST keeps only semantic content—no parens nodes, no single-child pass-through nodes.

practiceProblems.title: Complex Expression Parsing
practiceProblems.explanation: Function calls are nodes with callee and arguments. Precedence makes g(c)*3 a subtree before the addition.
hints: Function calls are AST nodes too

minigame.title: AST Architect
minigame.description: Build Abstract Syntax Trees by dragging and connecting nodes! Learn how precedence, associativity, and parentheses shape the tree structure. A fun puzzle game for understanding parser output.
instructions: Read the expression at the top
Drag operators and operands to build the tree
Higher precedence operators go deeper in the tree
Connect nodes by dragging from parent to child
Submit when your tree matches the expression semantics

visualizer.title: Parser & AST Builder
visualizer.description: Watch recursive descent parsing in action. See tokens transform into a hierarchical tree. Observe how precedence rules shape the tree structure.
